summary: Describes the format to use for sending Apple Macintosh files via MIME. These files have two parts, so the format keeps both when they travel by email. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Mac files have two halves. This note says how to package both halves in an email so they arrive together.

subtitle: How to mail a two-part Macintosh file through MIME without losing either part.

tldr.problem: A Macintosh file has two parts, a data fork and a resource fork, plus extra Finder information. Ordinary mail and non-Macintosh systems handle only one stream of data, so sending the whole file safely was awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the MIME types application/applefile and multipart/appledouble. In the preferred AppleDouble form the Macintosh-specific parts travel in one body part and the plain data fork in another, labeled with its normal content type.
tldr.outcome: Macintosh recipients get the whole document, while other users can easily extract the data fork. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 1740 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Macintosh Files Are Different
sections.content:
A Macintosh file consists of two parts called forks. The data fork holds the actual data and is typically the only meaningful part on a non-Macintosh computer. The resource fork holds a collection of arbitrary attribute/value pairs, including program segments, icon bitmaps and parametric values. The Finder also keeps more information about each file in a hidden file called the Desktop Database.

A filesystem on another kind of computer stores consecutive data in one part, so it is common to convert a Macintosh file into some other format before sending it over a network. This memo describes how to do that inside MIME mail, in a way that is compatible with existing ways of distributing Macintosh files while giving non-Macintosh systems access to data in standard formats.
sections.eli5: A Mac file has a main part and a helper part with things like icons. Other computers only understand the main part, so mailing the whole file needs a plan.

sections.title: AppleSingle and AppleDouble
sections.content:
Two Apple formats are used, both described in an Apple developer's note. AppleSingle encodes a Macintosh file as one byte stream. AppleDouble is similar, except that the data fork is separated from the Macintosh-specific parts.

AppleDouble is the preferred format for a Macintosh file in an Internet mail message. Recipients with Macintosh computers get the entire document, including icons and other Macintosh-specific information, while other users can easily extract the data fork because it is separate from the AppleDouble encoding.
sections.eli5: AppleSingle packs everything in one bag. AppleDouble uses two bags, so people who only want the main part can grab it without opening the other one.

sections.title: Choosing a Format
sections.content:
Not every Macintosh document needs special treatment. A document with a well-known MIME type and a non-existent or trivial resource fork can be sent as a regular MIME body part, with no AppleSingle or AppleDouble at all.

A document that lacks a data fork must be sent as AppleSingle. Unless there are strong reasons not to, every other document should normally be sent as AppleDouble. That includes documents with non-trivial resource forks and documents without a corresponding well-known MIME type. The RFC adds that it may be valuable to let the user choose one format over another, for example because the user disagrees with the implementor's idea of a trivial resource fork.
sections.eli5: If a file is plain, just send it normally. If it has no main part, use one bag. For most other Mac files, use two bags.

sections.title: The MIME Types and Their Use
sections.content:
The RFC registers two types. application/applefile carries AppleSingle data, or the header half of AppleDouble. It has no required parameters and an optional NAME parameter, which must be a value as defined in RFC 1521. Because it contains binary data it will typically need Content-Transfer-Encoding: BASE64. multipart/appledouble has the same parameters and no encoding considerations.

An AppleSingle file is sent as the one and only part, in an application/applefile message. An AppleDouble file is sent as a multipart/appledouble body part that may have only two sub-parts: the header (resource fork and desktop information) as application/applefile, and the data fork as whatever type best describes it, for example image/gif. If no suitable type is registered, the data fork goes out as application/octet-stream.

The first four bytes of an AppleSingle header are, in hexadecimal, 00, 05, 16, 00. For an AppleDouble header they are 00, 05, 16, 07. The safest transfer encoding is Base64, since it works over the most restricted channels. A name parameter is recommended to hint at the file being attached, but since its value must be a value from RFC 1521 it is limited to seven-bit US-ASCII characters.
sections.eli5: The email says which kind of bag it is with a label. The Mac helper part gets one label, and the main part gets whatever label fits, like picture or plain bytes.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a one-line AppleSingle example, Content-Type: application/applefile; name="Computers-1/2-93", followed by the AppleSingle file.

Its AppleDouble example uses multipart/appledouble with the boundary mac-part. The first part is the application/applefile header with the name My-new-car. The second part is the data fork, here labeled image/gif.
sections.eli5: The example shows an email with two parts: the Mac helper part first, then the picture itself.

sections.title: Inside the AppleSingle Header
sections.content:
Appendix A summarizes the Apple format. A file is a header followed by one or more data entries, each of which is optional. The header has a magic number (4 bytes), a version number (4 bytes), a filler (16 bytes) and a number of entries (2 bytes). Each entry then has a descriptor with an Entry ID, an Offset and a Length, 4 bytes each. Fields use MC68000 byte order, most significant byte first.

The magic number is 0x00051600 for AppleSingle and 0x00051607 for AppleDouble, so an application can tell whether it must look elsewhere for the data fork. The version described is 0x00020000. Entry IDs run from 1 to $FFFFFFFF, with 0 invalid. Apple reserves 1 to $7FFFFFFF, and the rest is free for applications to define.

An AppleDouble header file has the same format as AppleSingle but has no data fork entry. Apple recommends placing the resource fork entry last, because it is the entry most commonly extended after the data fork. Appendix C is a C header file, applefile.h, showing structures for parsing both formats.
sections.eli5: The header is a table of contents. It says what kind of file this is and where each piece, like the icon or the main data, starts and how long it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC gives one caution. To the extent that application/applefile carries operating-system sensitive data, it may open a door for easier relaxation of security rules than the sender, or the administrator of the sender's system, intended.
sections.eli5: The Mac helper part carries special information about the computer, which could let something slip through that the sender did not mean to allow.

fields.name: Number of entries
fields.desc: How many entry descriptors follow; an unsigned 16-bit number.

data.title: AppleDouble message
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/appledouble; boundary=mac-part

--mac-part
Content-Type: application/applefile; name="My-new-car"

    [The AppleDouble header goes here]

--mac-part
Content-Type: image/gif;

    [The data fork goes here]

--mac-part--
